title: Self-Esteem, Shame & the Inner Critic
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

glossary.definition: Treating a success or mistake as a verdict about the whole person.

For example: After receiving feedback, somebody wishes they could disappear from the class.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Izzy received useful criticism on a design task. Morgan finds her considering whether to abandon the course.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of self-worth; Gilbert (1998), Shame.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling ashamed is not proof that the criticism was deserved, and improving a skill does not require permanently feeling confident.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of self-worth; Gilbert (1998), Shame.
nodes.scenario: Izzy received useful criticism on a design task. Morgan finds her considering whether to abandon the course.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The tutor said my layout was confusing.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Did they criticise the whole project or one part of it?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: One part. But if I can't do something this basic, what does that say about me?

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What did the feedback actually ask you to change?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Feeling ashamed is not proof that the criticism was deserved, and improving a skill does not require permanently feeling confident.
checks.counterexample: Feeling ashamed is not proof that the criticism was deserved, and improving a skill does not require permanently feeling confident.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling ashamed is not proof that the criticism was deserved, and improving a skill does not require permanently feeling confident.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of self-worth; Gilbert (1998), Shame.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Izzy turns specific performance feedback into a global judgement of herself. This broad evaluation can make ordinary learning tasks feel like tests of personal worth.

Another possibility: The teaching may be unsupportive or the feedback excessively harsh, which would change the meaning and impact of the experience.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of self-worth; Gilbert (1998), Shame.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Compare the exact scope of the criticism with the scope of the conclusion Izzy draws about herself. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling ashamed is not proof that the criticism was deserved, and improving a skill does not require permanently feeling confident.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of self-worth; Gilbert (1998), Shame.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Compare the exact scope of the criticism with the scope of the conclusion Izzy draws about herself.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: The tutor's written feedback praises three other elements and says the layout is 'promising with two correctable weaknesses'.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of self-worth; Gilbert (1998), Shame.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The written record weakens the notion that the tutor evaluated Izzy as generally incompetent. Her global interpretation now becomes a more important target for examination.
nodes.counterexample: Feeling ashamed is not proof that the criticism was deserved, and improving a skill does not require permanently feeling confident.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of self-worth; Gilbert (1998), Shame.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of Self-Worth.
nodes.scenario: Hal has failed a presentation component of a training assessment.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I failed the case presentation. Maybe I shouldn't be in this field.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What did the assessors actually say?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The formulation was clear, but I rushed the risk section.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: So there's a part to practise.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: It feels like everybody can see I'm just not good enough.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Would a better risk section change what you think of yourself?

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Hal is concerned that the assessment procedure was unfair.
Hal may be treating a specific skill deficit as evidence of globally inadequate worth.
The assessment exposed a meaningful gap in Hal's risk-formulation skill.
The teaching may be unsupportive or the feedback excessively harsh, which would change the meaning and impact of the experience.
options.feedback: This is a plausible competing hypothesis. Its relative strength depends on whether it accounts for the most revealing details.

options.label: Izzy turns specific performance feedback into a global judgement of herself. This broad evaluation can make ordinary learning tasks feel like tests of personal worth.
options.feedback: A process formulation may fit, but the evidence may also support other contributors.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Hal may be treating a specific skill deficit as evidence of globally inadequate worth. The assessment exposed a meaningful gap in Hal's risk-formulation skill. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: The assessment may reveal a genuine weakness. Accurate feedback and a less global judgement can coexist.

checks.prompt: You are Hal. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Practise the risk section using the feedback while treating the result as evidence about that skill.
options.reply: Could the same standard apply to you?
options.consequence: The conversation may not be solved, but the immediate problem now has a concrete route forward.

options.label: Avoid talking about the mark until you feel confident about yourself again.
options.reply: Would a better risk section change what you think of yourself?
options.consequence: Backing away can ease pressure now while leaving the original concern unresolved.

options.label: Before making any decision, I'd like you to explain exactly why you responded that way.
options.reply: So there's a part to practise.
options.consequence: Demanding a definitive motive may provoke another defence rather than settle the issue.

options.label: Let's ask someone else to intervene before discussing this further.
options.reply: What would you tell another trainee with the same feedback?
options.consequence: Independent help can be appropriate when direct discussion fails or safety requires it; timing matters.

options.label: The teaching may be unsupportive or the feedback excessively harsh, which would change the meaning and impact of the experience.
options.feedback: This is a plausible competing hypothesis. Its relative strength depends on whether it accounts for the most revealing details.

checks.explanation: The first response addresses what can change. Asking about motives may help eventually; it need not be resolved before the concrete issue can be addressed.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
After receiving a 'needs development' rating in one skill, an employee concludes that their colleagues must see them as fundamentally inadequate.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Izzy turns specific performance feedback into a global judgement of herself. This broad evaluation can make ordinary learning tasks feel like tests of personal worth.

Feeling ashamed is not proof that the criticism was deserved, and improving a skill does not require permanently feeling confident.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Crocker & Wolfe (2001), Contingencies of self-worth; Gilbert (1998), Shame.

glossary.definition: A judgement about how well a particular task was done at a particular time.
glossary.example: A tutor says the order of information on a chart is confusing.
glossary.limit: Criticism of a piece of work does not directly measure the value of its author.

glossary.definition: Treating a success or mistake as a verdict about the whole person.
glossary.example: One confusing chart becomes proof that somebody is generally incompetent.
glossary.limit: One domain gives too little evidence for a conclusion about the whole self.

glossary.definition: A painful feeling that the self is flawed or exposed to rejection.
glossary.example: After receiving feedback, somebody wishes they could disappear from the class.
glossary.limit: Shame can occur even when criticism was limited or unfair.

glossary.definition: Responding to difficulty with accuracy and care rather than contempt.
glossary.example: I made a mistake in the layout; I can correct it without calling myself worthless.
glossary.limit: Self-compassion allows accountability; it does not mean denying errors.
